reference: EN 442-2 emitter characteristic Phi = Phi_50 (dT_ln/49.83)^n with the logarithmic mean excess temperature, and the EN 1264 basic characteristic q = 8.92 (theta_F,m - theta_i)^1.1 with its inversion and the standard floor surface caps, both implemented in python from the published equations; the plant, hydraulic and degree-day arithmetic is recomputed independently as closed-form identities.
reference_citations: EN 442-2, "Radiators and convectors - Part 2: Test methods and rating": nominal thermal output measured at 75/65/20 degC and converted with Phi = Phi_50 (dT_ln/dT_ln,50)^n.

P. Sarbu et al. / L. Bagi et al., "Can we still trust in EN 442? New operating definitions for radiators, Part 1 and Part 2", REHVA Journal (2022): states the EN 442-2 conversion as Phi = Phi_50 (dT_ln/dT_ln,50)^n and the design point "75-65-20 degC, which means 50 K (dT_ln = 49.83 K) over-temperature"; reports measured exponents n = 1.26...1.35 and deviations up to about 10 % at reduced mass flow / increased spread. https://www.rehva.eu/rehva-journal/chapter/can-we-still-trust-in-en-442-new-operating-definitions-for-radiators-part-2-model-based-analysis-and-results

buildingservicestutor.com, "Hydronic balancing step 4: calculate radiator output": confirms the logarithmic excess temperature convention and the 75/65/20 reference, and quotes n = 1.3 for panel radiators, 1.26 for towel radiators. https://www.buildingservicestutor.com/calculate-radiator-output/
DIN EN 1264 basic characteristic curve for floor heating, q = 8.92 (theta_F,m - theta_i)^1.1 W/m2, as quoted at https://www.hilfreiche-tools.de/waermestromdichte-fussbodenheizung/

EN 1264 floor surface temperature limits 29 degC (occupied zone), 35 degC (peripheral zone) and 33 degC (bathrooms), as quoted in Uponor, "Underfloor heating and cooling - planning principles", https://brandportal.uponor.com/m/7187327a41365ace/original/TI-planning-principles-UFHC-EN-1186660-v1.pdf
tolerance: The tool states which published closed forms it implements, so the reference implements the same forms independently in python and the tool is held to 1e-9 relative on every continuous quantity; volumes the tool rounds to whole litres and unit counts must match exactly. Two things are deliberately not graded to a tighter number than the physics allows: the reference temperature difference, where the exact logarithmic mean at 75/65/20 is 49.83289 K and the tool - like the industry - declares 49.83, a 0.006 % rounding whose effect on the output factor is 0.008 %, and the unity check at the rating point, which is therefore given 2e-4. The arithmetic-mean variant of the same law is computed alongside every case and its distance from the logarithmic one recorded (up to 8.9 % over the regime grid) so that the convention actually in use is demonstrated rather than assumed.
not_benchmarked: The EN 442 exponents themselves. They are per-type generics (1.30 radiator, 1.35 convector, 1.25 radiant panel, 1.00 fan coil) inside the published 1.26-1.35 band for radiators, but a certified value belongs to a model, not to a type; the harness checks the law is applied faithfully, not that 1.30 is right for a given radiator.

The known weakness of the EN 442 logarithmic conversion itself: REHVA (2022) measured deviations up to about 10 % at strongly reduced mass flow and increased spread, and proposes an additional (dT_ar/dT_ar,50)^g factor. The tool does not apply that correction; its absence is now disclosed but its magnitude is not graded here.

EN 1264-2 proper. The tool uses the basic characteristic curve q = 8.92 dT^1.1 and the surface caps, not the full product-coefficient method (B, a_B, a_T^mT, a_u^mu, a_D^mD); the mean water temperature is therefore a series-resistance simplification and is graded only for internal consistency (water hotter than the surface, inversion round-trip), not against EN 1264-2 dimensioning tables.

Wall heating, ceiling heating, cooled ceilings and concrete core activation. EN 1264-5 coefficients were not obtainable from a primary source for this pass, so wall heating is explicitly not dimensioned and the cooled-ceiling and concrete-core figures are indicative maxima that are not benchmarked.

The Carnot quality factors per source type, the 0.88 defrost penalty, the 0.022/K capacity derating slope, the 0.3/0.7 seasonal COP blend and the bivalent coverage curve are conventions of this tool with no published provenance; only their faithful and consistent application is checked.

The building profiles, the 66 rule texts and the report layout are editorial content, not computation; only the three emitter-threshold rules and the wall-heating rule are checked against the numbers they quote.
The load itself: it is entered or derived from a W/m2 rule of thumb, not computed to EN 12831.

The glycol correction c_p x (1 - 0.0045 f) and rho x (1 + 0.0009 f) is a linear fit with no stated provenance and no brine type; it is applied consistently and the flow identity is checked with it, but the fit itself is not graded against glycol property tables.
run_notes: Driven through the tool's own permalink codec; every number read back from Diagram.record.build().

Baseline before this pass: the mean water temperature of a heated floor was computed as theta_i + q R_covering, which put the water COLDER than the floor surface it was supposed to heat for every default case (at 87.5 W/m2 with R = 0.09 m2K/W: surface 27.97 degC, water 27.88 degC). It is now built up from the EN 1264 surface temperature plus the drop across the covering and the screed. The bivalent point came from a 0.1 K stepped scan that returned a value up to 0.1 K low with visible floating-point drift (0.7999999999999846 instead of 0.80597); it is now solved exactly. The pipe-spacing answer was read from the form and then never passed to the calculation, so changing it moved nothing; this benchmark found that and it is now wired through. Wall heating could be selected and produced no calculation and no message at all.

The exact logarithmic mean excess temperature at 75/65/20 is 49.83289 K; the tool declares 49.83. The two differ by 0.006 %, which moves the output factor by 0.008 % - below the display resolution of every figure that uses it.
crosscheck: logarithmic vs arithmetic mean excess temperature over the 14-regime grid: the two conventions differ by 0.0 % at the rating point and by up to 8.9 % at 45/30/20. The tool follows the logarithmic convention that EN 442-2 prescribes.
